newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Voting starts in ex-Soviet Moldova.
newsitem.headline: Voting starts in ex-Soviet Moldova.

text.p: Moldovans began voting on Sunday in their first multi-party presidential election, hotly contested by three top state officials -- the president, the prime minister and the chairman of parliament.
Nearly 2,000 polling stations opened at 8 a.m. (0600 GMT) across the ex-Soviet republic of 4.3 million people sandwiched between Romania and Ukraine. Voting lasts 12 hours.
The election law says more than 50 percent of the 2.4 million eligible voters have to take part to make the poll valid but experts expect a much higher turnout.
In the capital Chisinau a steady flow of people headed for the polling stations which, in a Soviet tradition, offered the voters well-stocked and cheap buffets.
"I want a better future," said Andrei, a 78-year-old ethnic Russian pensioner. "I want the leaders who work and I do not want the people to live in poverty."
He refused to say for whom he had voted, but said he had chosen one of the three front-runners -- President Mircea Snegur, Prime Minister Angrei Sangheli and Parliament Chairman Petru Lucinschi.

There are six other candidates, including the head of the Communist Party and a radical nationalist. Experts expect none of the candidates to win more than 50 percent of the vote in the first round and predict a run-off between the two top contenders on December 1.
Snegur, 56, elected in 1991, led an aggressive and populist campaign, saying he needed more powers for the next term to improve people's lives.
He has angered his opponents by promising to dissolve Sangheli's government which he called "corrupt" and Lucinschi's parliament and to turn Moldova into a presidential republic.
Snegur, backed by several nationalist groups, wants closer ties with the West and Romania, with which Moldova shares a common language and culture.
Sangheli, 52, who prides himself for his International Monetary Fund economic stabilisation programme, is leaning towards Russia, Moldova's main market and energy supplier.
Lucinschi, the 52-year-old charismatic intellectual and former communist leader of Soviet Molodova, has campaigned as a moderate, social democratic centrist.
Preliminary results of Sunday's vote are expected on Monday.

The breakaway Dnestr region has banned voting on its territory but voters may vote outside the area. The region, populated mainly by Ukrainians and Russians, broke away in 1992, fearing a possible merger between Moldova and Romania.
